brief.topic: Why Six Multiplications Return to One

s01: Multiply three by itself six times.
The result is seven hundred twenty nine, which leaves remainder one when divided by seven.
Why should that happen?
Look at the six nonzero remainders: one through six.
Multiply each by three, then take the remainder after dividing by seven.
We get three, six, two, five, one, four.
The order changed, but the collection did not.
Multiplication by three permutes the nonzero remainders.
Multiply every entry in each row.
The lower product is the upper product times six copies of three, modulo seven.
But the rows contain exactly the same factors.
We can cancel their common product because none of its factors is divisible by the prime seven.
What remains says three to the sixth leaves remainder one.
The same argument works with any nonzero remainder modulo a prime.
Multiplication cannot merge two remainders, because a prime dividing their multiplied difference must divide the difference itself.
This is Fermat's little theorem.
The prime condition matters.
Modulo six, multiplying one through five by two creates repeats and a zero.
Two to the fifth leaves remainder two, not one.
The rearrangement proof tells us both why the theorem works and where it breaks.

scenes.narration:
Multiply three by itself six times. The result is seven hundred twenty nine, which leaves remainder one when divided by seven. Why should that happen?

Look at the six nonzero remainders: one through six. Multiply each by three, then take the remainder after dividing by seven. We get three, six, two, five, one, four.

The order changed, but the collection did not. Multiplication by three permutes the nonzero remainders.

Multiply every entry in each row. The lower product is the upper product times six copies of three, modulo seven. But the rows contain exactly the same factors.

We can cancel their common product because none of its factors is divisible by the prime seven. What remains says three to the sixth leaves remainder one.

The same argument works with any nonzero remainder modulo a prime. Multiplication cannot merge two remainders, because a prime dividing their multiplied difference must divide the difference itself. This is Fermat's little theorem.

The prime condition matters. Modulo six, multiplying one through five by two creates repeats and a zero. Two to the fifth leaves remainder two, not one. The rearrangement proof tells us both why the theorem works and where it breaks.
